title: Collecting Fine Italian Wine
quiz.0.question: Which Italian wine is most valued at international auctions?
quiz.0.explanation: Barolo Riserva from top estates (such as Giacomo Conterno and Bruno Giacosa) performs best at international auctions, with long ageing potential and small production, making it one of the most sought-after Italian wines at auction.
quiz.1.question: What type of oak do traditionalist Barolo producers use?
quiz.1.explanation: Traditionalists (tradizionalisti) use large Slavonian oak casks (botti), letting the wine evolve slowly; the wines need long ageing and are the first choice of old-wine collectors.
quiz.2.question: Which estate founded Brunello di Montalcino?
quiz.2.explanation: Biondi-Santi founded Brunello di Montalcino: in the late 19th century Ferruccio Biondi-Santi established the tradition of making long-lived red wine from Sangiovese, and historic old vintages are prized by collectors.
quiz.3.question: Which wine is the best starting point for a beginner collector?
quiz.3.options.0: Buy the oldest Barolo vintages straight away
quiz.3.options.1: Chianti Classico Gran Selezione from well-known estates
quiz.3.explanation: Beginners are advised to start with Chianti Classico Gran Selezione from well-known estates: relatively reasonable prices, consistent quality and some ageing potential, building appreciation before moving up to Barolo/Brunello.
quiz.4.question: What is the defining feature of Giacomo Conterno's Monfortino?
quiz.4.options.0: Short ageing in small French barriques only
quiz.4.options.1: A Barolo Riserva made only in outstanding vintages and aged for a long time in large oak casks
quiz.4.options.3: Made in the same quantity every year
quiz.4.explanation: Monfortino is Giacomo Conterno's flagship Barolo Riserva, made only in outstanding vintages, with a long traditional maceration and years of ageing in large botti; it is seen as the archetype of traditional Barolo.
quiz.5.question: What was the background to the birth of the Super Tuscans?
quiz.5.options.0: The 1950s, as Italy began copying France by planting international varieties
quiz.5.options.1: The 1970s, as winemakers frustrated with outdated DOC rules broke away to innovate
quiz.5.options.2: The 1990s, as globalisation internationalised Italian wine
quiz.5.options.3: The 2000s, as the organic movement promoted diversity of varieties
quiz.5.explanation: Super Tuscans were born in the 1970s. Antinori's Tignanello (first made in 1971) left out white grapes and added Cabernet Sauvignon, breaking the Chianti DOC rules of the time, so it could only be sold as vino da tavola; Sassicaia (Tenuta San Guido, first released in 1968) rose at the same time. It was winemakers frustrated with traditional rules, willingly declassifying their wines, who created this category that changed the history of Italian wine.
quiz.6.question: When assessing a collection of top Italian wine, what is the key meaning of "provenance"?
quiz.6.options.0: That the wine was made in Italy, not imported
quiz.6.options.1: The full storage history of the wine from the estate to today, the core basis for auction houses to judge authenticity and quality
quiz.6.options.2: Historical documents about the vineyard — the older the better
quiz.6.options.3: The licence to sell the wine in Italy
quiz.6.explanation: Provenance is the full chain of custody of a wine: from release by the estate, through intermediate merchants and storage records, to the current owner. Without clear provenance, even a genuine bottle may be refused or heavily marked down by auction houses; it is the core safeguard against counterfeits and quality problems.
slides.0.title: Collecting Fine Italian Wine
slides.0.subtitle: Core strategies for collecting Barolo, Brunello and Amarone
slides.1.title: Why Collect Top Italian Wine?
slides.1.content:
Top Italian wine is an important part of the international collectors' market: scarcity, ageing potential and reputation together support the long-term value of the finest wines. But wine prices fluctuate, so collecting should centre on drinking and appreciation rather than being treated as a guaranteed investment.

Scarcity: top single vineyards (MGAs) and flagship wines of great estates are made in limited quantities, and demand often exceeds supply
Ageing potential: top Barolo / Brunello can age for decades, with complexity continuing to develop
Brand power: top estates such as Giacomo Conterno and Gaja enjoy global fame and steady secondary-market demand
slides.2.title: Three Top Collectible Wines
slides.2.content:
Barolo DOCG — The King of Italy

Grape: 100% Nebbiolo | Minimum ageing: 38 months (Riserva 62 months)
Top estates for collectors: Giacomo Conterno (Monfortino), Gaja, Bruno Giacosa, Bartolo Mascarello
Highlights: decades of ageing potential, scarce MGA single vineyards, legendary vintages in high demand

Brunello di Montalcino DOCG — A Tuscan Legend

Grape: 100% Sangiovese (locally called Brunello) | Minimum ageing: 5 years (Riserva 6 years)
Top estates for collectors: Biondi-Santi (the founder), Soldera, Poggio di Sotto, Ciacci Piccolomini
Highlights: high global profile, frequent auction sales, old Biondi-Santi vintages repeatedly set auction records

Amarone della Valpolicella DOCG — King of Richness

Grapes: mainly Corvina, with Rondinella | Made from dried grapes (appassimento), dried for several months
Top estates for collectors: Dal Forno Romano (tiny production), Quintarelli, old vintages of Bertani
Highlights: tiny production from top estates, high alcohol and strong structure, long ageing potential
slides.3.title: Judging Estates: Traditionalists vs Modernists
slides.3.content:
When choosing estates to collect, it helps to understand Italy's two main winemaking philosophies — traditionalists and modernists differ sharply in style and ageing potential, and market preferences shift in cycles.

Traditionalists (Tradizionalisti)

  • Examples: Giacomo Conterno, Bartolo Mascarello, Bruno Giacosa
  • Oak: large Slavonian oak casks (botti), slow oxidative evolution
  • Maceration: long macerations of several weeks, extracting plenty of tannin
  • Ageing: needs long ageing, the first choice of old-wine collectors
  • Market: highly sought after at auction, with strong demand for rare old vintages

Modernists (the Barolo Boys)

  • Examples: Gaja, Elio Altare, Roberto Voerzio, Luciano Sandrone
  • Oak: small French barriques (225 L), adding vanilla and coffee notes
  • Maceration: shorter macerations, approachable earlier
  • Ageing: reaches its drinking window earlier, with rich fruit
  • Market: Gaja has huge international recognition, an entry choice for new collectors
slides.4.title: Profiles of the Great Estates
slides.4.content:
🏆 Giacomo Conterno — The Summit of Barolo

Flagship: Barolo Monfortino Riserva | From: the Cascina Francia vineyard in Serralunga d'Alba (bought in 1974)
Scarcity: made only in outstanding vintages; in weaker years it is not released at all
Ageing philosophy: long traditional maceration, then years in large botti before bottling, so it is already well aged on release
Market position: regarded as the archetypal traditional Barolo, pursued by collectors and at auction

🌹 Biondi-Santi — The Origin of Brunello

Flagship: Brunello di Montalcino Riserva | Ferruccio Biondi-Santi defined the style of Brunello in the late 19th century (the 1888 vintage is often seen as the starting point)
Historical significance: made Montalcino famous with Brunello able to age for decades, and the estate still keeps historic old vintages
Today: since 2016 the French EPI group has held a majority stake, raising its international profile

🍇 Dal Forno Romano — The Holy Grail of Amarone

Flagship: Amarone della Valpolicella | Location: the Illasi valley (east of Verona, in the eastern part of Valpolicella)
Scarcity: small production and strict allocation, so little reaches the market
Style: extremely concentrated and massive, ranked with Quintarelli as the most sought-after Amarone
slides.5.title: Collecting Super Tuscans
slides.5.content:
Super Tuscans were born in the 1970s by breaking with traditional rules, and are now among Italy's most internationally recognised collectible wines, alongside Barolo / Brunello.

Sassicaia (Tenuta San Guido)

Bolgheri Sassicaia DOC · mainly Cabernet Sauvignon, with Cabernet Franc

In 1994 it became Italy's first DOC covering a single estate. It rose to fame when the 1972 vintage beat several great Bordeaux wines in a 1978 Decanter blind tasting, and it is one of the benchmarks for Italian wine on the international market.

Ornellaia (Tenuta dell'Ornellaia)

Bolgheri Superiore DOC · mainly Cabernet Sauvignon, blended with Merlot, Cabernet Franc and others

Founded in 1981 by Lodovico Antinori and now part of the Frescobaldi group. A Bordeaux-style blend; each year its "Vendemmia d'Artista" (artist's vintage) brings a limited-edition label, a series followed closely by collectors.

Masseto

Toscana IGT · 100% Merlot, in a Bordeaux Right Bank style

One of Italy's most expensive Merlots, often called "Italy's Pétrus". Originally a wine of Ornellaia, it has been a separate estate since 2019.

Tignanello (Marchesi Antinori)

Toscana IGT · mainly Sangiovese + Cabernet Sauvignon + Cabernet Franc

A Super Tuscan icon and pioneer (first made in 1971), easier to obtain than other top wines and a good starting point for building a collection.
slides.6.title: Managing Risk and Avoiding Pitfalls
slides.6.content:
The risks of collecting wine should not be ignored — counterfeits, poor storage and lack of market liquidity are the three core risks. Knowing how to guard against them protects the long-term value of a collection.

⚠️ Counterfeit Risk

High-risk wines: Giacomo Conterno Monfortino, Biondi-Santi Riserva, Dal Forno Amarone — the most common targets of counterfeiters
Safeguards: ① buy from reputable importers or auction houses; ② check the serial number on the DOCG fascetta; ③ check the estate's original wooden case (OWC) and release batch records
What to check: label print quality, the branding on the cork, and whether the capsule version matches the vintage; use a third-party authentication service when needed

🌡️ Storage Risk

Most common mistake: sharp temperature swings and excessive heat both damage wine and harm the cork over time
Solution: store valuable wines in a professional bonded warehouse and keep complete storage records, which auction houses accept more readily
Storing at home: if valuable wines are kept at home, keep temperature and humidity records; wines without storage records may be valued lower at auction

📊 Liquidity Risk

Illiquid wines: wines from lesser-known areas, with low scores, little recognition or very large production are hard to sell quickly on the secondary market
Strategy: focus most of the budget on well-known core wines with a solid secondary-market trading record (Barolo, Brunello, top Super Tuscans)
Diversification: spread across three dimensions — different wines (Barolo + Brunello + Super Tuscan), different vintages (legendary + excellent) and different price levels (flagships + second wines)
slides.7.title: Three Levels of Collecting
slides.7.content:
Beginner

Build Your Palate

  • Chianti Classico Gran Selezione, standard Barolo and Brunello
  • Compare 3-5 vintages side by side, using a temperature-controlled wine fridge (about 12°C)
  • Most of these wines are best within 5-15 years
Intermediate

Single Vineyards and Verticals

  • Barolo MGA single vineyards, Brunello Riserva, top Amarone
  • Vertical collections (many vintages from one estate) to compare vintages
  • Buy directly from estates, reputable importers or auction houses
Top Level

Rare Old Vintages

  • Giacomo Conterno Monfortino, old Biondi-Santi Riserva, Quintarelli Amarone
  • Favour wines in original wooden cases (OWC) with full provenance documents
  • Buy through major auction houses, with close attention to storage records
slides.8.title: Key Takeaways
slides.8.points.0: The three drivers of collecting top Italian wine: scarcity (MGA single vineyards), ageing potential (decades) and brand power
slides.8.points.1: The three top collectible wines: Barolo DOCG (the king of Italy), Brunello di Montalcino DOCG, Amarone della Valpolicella DOCG
slides.8.points.2: Wine prices fluctuate with the market; collecting should centre on drinking and appreciation rather than being treated as a guaranteed investment
slides.8.points.3: Monfortino is made only in outstanding vintages and aged for a long time in large casks, the archetype of traditional Barolo
slides.8.points.4: Biondi-Santi defined the style of Brunello; since 2016 the EPI group has held a majority stake
slides.8.points.5: Dal Forno Romano and Quintarelli are the most sought-after Amarone producers, with small production and strict allocation
slides.8.points.6: Super Tuscan collectibles: Sassicaia (the first single-estate DOC, 1994), Masseto (Italy's Pétrus, independent since 2019), Ornellaia (limited artist's-vintage labels)
slides.8.points.7: Tignanello (first made in 1971) is a Super Tuscan pioneer, relatively easy to obtain and a good starting point for a collection
slides.8.points.8: The three risks: counterfeits (guard with the fascetta + OWC + provenance), poor storage (use professional storage and keep records), illiquidity (focus on well-known wines with a trading record)

slides.9.questions.0.question: Which Italian wine is most valued at international auctions?
slides.9.questions.0.explanation: Barolo Riserva from top estates (such as Giacomo Conterno and Bruno Giacosa) performs best at international auctions, with long ageing potential and small production, making it one of the most sought-after Italian wines at auction.
slides.9.questions.1.question: What type of oak do traditionalist Barolo producers use?
slides.9.questions.1.explanation: Traditionalists (tradizionalisti) use large Slavonian oak casks (botti), letting the wine evolve slowly, and are the first choice of old-wine collectors.
slides.9.questions.2.question: Which estate founded Brunello di Montalcino?
slides.9.questions.2.explanation: Biondi-Santi founded Brunello di Montalcino: in the late 19th century Ferruccio Biondi-Santi established the tradition of making long-lived red wine from Sangiovese.
slides.9.questions.3.question: Masseto is called "Italy's Pétrus". Which grape is it made from?
slides.9.questions.3.explanation: Masseto is made from 100% Merlot; on clay plots in Bolgheri it shows a style rivalling Bordeaux's Right Bank (Pomerol/Pétrus), and it is one of Italy's most expensive single-variety reds.
slides.9.questions.4.question: When assessing top Italian wines for a collection, what is the role of the DOCG fascetta?
slides.9.questions.4.options.0: Shows the wine's best drinking years
slides.9.questions.4.options.1: A unique officially issued serial number, the most reliable external sign of a genuine DOCG
slides.9.questions.4.options.3: Shows that export duty has been paid
slides.9.questions.4.explanation: The fascetta is the official anti-counterfeiting seal every bottle of DOCG wine must carry, printed with a unique serial number and usually placed across the neck; it is the most reliable external tool for verifying a DOCG and an important basis for auction houses assessing provenance.
slides.9.questions.5.question: Where does the scarcity of Dal Forno Romano's Amarone mainly come from?
slides.9.questions.5.options.1: Small production and strict allocation by the estate, so very little reaches the market
slides.9.questions.5.options.2: Vines over 200 years old with naturally tiny yields
slides.9.questions.5.options.3: It is made only in odd-numbered years
slides.9.questions.5.explanation: Dal Forno Romano makes little wine and strictly controls its allocation, so very little circulates on the market or the secondary market, which makes it highly sought after at auction.
